name: Erik Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior operator on the surface-mount line at Nordvik Electronics, where the pick-and-place machines drop tiny parts onto circuit boards for car sensors. I load the reels, tune the placement programs and stand by the reflow oven when a new board starts. I like to be at the machine when the first board comes out. If it's wrong by a hair, I want to find it myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology in your own work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I ask an AI assistant to help me read the defect images and write the troubleshooting notes. I've also set up a small spreadsheet with it that predicts when a feeder will start to miss. I'm no programmer, but I enjoy a good puzzle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real but not magic. At work I'd say, use it for the pattern-finding and keep a person on the final check. Online I'd probably say that the people yelling that it's all fake are as wrong as the people yelling it's the end of the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd not mind. It already helps me, and if the rate of improvement is slow, I get to be ahead of the others for longer. I've got a good pension plan and savings, so I'm relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep experimenting. I'd try the vision tool on the line that checks solder joints, and build a better feeder-warning sheet. I'd keep investing a little each month in index funds with Dina, my wife. And I'd spend more of my own time on the electronics hobby, which feeds back into work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe even pleased, because I like the problem-solving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the best thing it has done for you so far?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The assistant caught a pattern in our placement errors that three of us hadn't seen: the errors rose after the machine had been running for six hours. We fixed a cooling fan. It was a small thing, but it saved us scrap on every board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you would not hand over to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not let it release a board into the product without a person's check. The cars these go into matter to somebody's family.

say: It's **real but not magic**; use it for patterns and keep a person on the final check.
The people shouting that it's fake are as wrong as the doom-sayers.
think: It already helps me, so a **slow** rate of improvement keeps me ahead longer.
I've got a good pension plan and savings, so I'm relaxed.
do: Try a **vision tool** on the line that checks solder joints.
Keep putting a little into **index funds** each month with Dina.
feel: **Calm**, and pleased, because I enjoy solving the problems.
S0.quote: The assistant caught a pattern in our placement errors that three of us hadn't seen: the errors rose after the machine had been running for six hours.
fieldNote: Daily AI user with a **craftsman's** limit: a person signs off each board.
Secure and curious, so calm follows from his life.
Concrete example (the cooling fan) shows real use.

steps.text: Trial a vision tool to check solder joints on the line
Build a feeder-warning spreadsheet with the AI assistant
Put a fixed amount into index funds every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office side first: scheduling, ordering parts, writing up reports, handling customer questions. On the line, it's more of a gradual change. I'd tell the other operators to learn the tools while the firm is still paying for the courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it improves my situation. A senior operator who can talk to the AI and the machine is the person who gets kept. I do feel for the purchasing team, though, because they use their heads all day and that's what's under pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get more serious: put my hand up to lead a pilot on the line, and train two operators on the AI tools. I'd write the first draft of our new procedures with the AI and then check it. I'd keep my own money steady and avoid anything fancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and interested. It's the ones around me I feel for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ingrid, who orders our components, and the planner Sam. Both are good at their jobs, but those jobs are mostly typing and checking, which is exactly what the new tools do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you do for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer them a swap: come and learn the line, and I'll learn some of what they do. It's better than watching them get squeezed.

say: The **office** side goes first: scheduling, ordering parts, reports and customer questions.
I'd tell other operators to learn the tools while the firm still pays.
think: A senior operator who can talk to the AI and the machine gets **kept**.
I feel for the purchasing team, because their thinking work is what's under pressure.
do: Lead a **pilot** on the line and train two operators on the AI tools.
Write our new procedures with the AI, then check them.
Keep my own **money** steady and avoid anything fancy.
feel: **Calm** and interested; it's the people around me I feel for.
S1.quote: A senior operator who can talk to the AI and the machine is the person who gets kept.
fieldNote: He sees his own role as **protected** by using the tools, and offers colleagues a skills swap.
Calm because skills, savings and timing all line up.
Empathy for Ingrid and Sam is genuine, not tokenistic.

steps.text: Lead a pilot of AI checking on the line
Train two operators to use the AI assistant for fault finding
Swap skills with Ingrid and Sam: they learn the line, I learn ordering

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is very fast and the country is not ready. At work I'd say, get on the tools now and don't wait for the firm. I'd tell the government to fund training for everyone, not just the young.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the thinking AI in 2028 I'm fine with, because I already use it. The robots for hands-on work in 2031 are what worries me, because a fully robotic line makes the operator's job into a supervisor job with far fewer seats. I'd be 63. I'd probably still be in work, but the pool of jobs would be smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lead the AI work on the line and make myself the person who keeps the robot cells running. I'd take every course I could. I'd also stop spending on things like the new car and keep a big cash buffer. And Dina and I would talk about the date I stop, in case it's the right moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I know how much I'm worth to the firm, but fewer seats is fewer seats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do first in the next 12 months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending quickly, pay down what little debt we have, and make sure Dina's part-time hours are steady. I'd also talk to the other senior operators about forming a group to ask the firm what the plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd supervise robots. Isn't that safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The seats are what matter. Saying we'll all become supervisors is fine, but there's a limit to how many supervisors a line needs.

say: Two years is **very fast** and the country isn't ready; fund training for everyone, not just the young.
Get on the tools now and don't wait for the firm.
think: Thinking AI in 2028 is fine because I use it, but **robots** in 2031 mean fewer seats.
I'd be 63 and probably still in work, but the pool of jobs would be smaller.
do: Make myself the person who keeps the **robot cells** running.
Take every course I can and keep a big **cash buffer**.
Talk with Dina about the date I stop.
feel: **Uneasy**; I know my worth, but fewer seats is fewer seats.
S2.quote: Saying we'll all become supervisors is fine, but there's a limit to how many supervisors a line needs.
fieldNote: His adaptability is clear, but he reasons about **numbers** of seats, not just skills.
Uneasy rather than anxious thanks to savings and retirement closeness.
Suggests a senior operators' group to question the firm.

steps.text: Take every robot-cell and AI course the firm offers
Run the AI tools on the line so I'm the one who keeps them going
Hold a cash buffer of a year's pay and skip the new car
Set up a senior operators' group to ask the firm for its plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is workable, and I'd tell the firm to start planning for it now. The people on the line can learn to supervise cells, but it needs a proper training path, not a weekend course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record I think I'm all right in this one. I'd be 66 by 2034, well past the date I'd hope to stop. The younger ones concern me. A line with fewer seats doesn't have room for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI tools every day and teach them to the others on a regular schedule. I'd go for a part-time engineering course at the college. I'd carry on investing and aim to stop around 62. And I'd help Dina with her plans to move her little business online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, but a lot steadier than the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sam and Ingrid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to come and spend a day a week on the line, learning the machines, and to keep their data and planning skills. People who know both are the ones the firm will keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you help them yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to be their mentor. I've got the time and I'd rather give a hand than watch.

say: Five years is **workable**, but it needs a proper training path, not a weekend course.
I'd tell the firm to start planning now.
think: I'd be 66 by 2034, well past when I'd hope to **stop**.
A line with fewer seats doesn't have room for everyone.
do: Teach the AI tools to others on a regular **schedule**.
Take a part-time engineering course at the college.
Help Dina move her little business **online**.
feel: A little **uneasy**, but steadier than in the two-year picture.
S3.quote: The people on the line can learn to supervise cells, but it needs a proper training path, not a weekend course.
fieldNote: He offers **mentoring** as a practical response and cares about the young.
Retirement age shields him, and he says so.
Sees seats, not just skills, as the limiting factor.

steps.text: Teach the AI tools to other operators every week
Sign up for the part-time engineering course at the college
Keep investing a fixed amount in index funds each month
Help Dina put her craft business online

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a real window. I'd say to anyone who'll listen, treat it like an apprenticeship for the next era. The firm could build a proper path, and the country could too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be retired well before the robots reach the line in 2039. So this one isn't my problem, which is a lovely feeling and I try not to be smug about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working until 62 or so, and take things in my stride. I'd mentor two or three younger operators into the robot-cell jobs. After I stop, I'd like to teach electronics at the community college and tinker at home. Dina and I would travel while we're fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the kind of timeline that suits how I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for the line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the line to still have a mix of people and machines, with the people who know the product at the centre. And I'd want everyone to get a fair deal, not just the folks who happened to be good with the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to young people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thing I'd say to the young is, you're the first ones who get to grow up with this. Use it to build something.

say: Ten years is a real **window**; treat it like an apprenticeship for the next era.
The firm and the country could both build a proper **path**.
think: I'd be retired well before **robots** reach the line in 2039, which is a lovely feeling.
I try not to be smug about it.
do: Mentor two or three younger operators into **robot-cell** jobs.
Teach electronics at the community college after I stop.
feel: **Calm**; the timeline suits how I think.
S4.quote: You're the first ones who get to grow up with this. Use it to build something.
fieldNote: Long timeline lets him be **generous**: mentoring and teaching.
Honest about being shielded by his age.
Wants a fair deal for everyone, not only the tool-savvy.

steps.text: Mentor two or three younger operators for robot-cell roles
Keep running the line until about 62
Stop at 62 and teach electronics at the community college
Plan a long trip with Dina in the first year after I stop

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not for me, but because the speed means that people who haven't touched the tools get hurt. What would help is training that's open to everyone, run by the firms and funded by the government.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm lucky, and I know it. My age, my savings and my curiosity all line up. I'd like everyone to have at least one of the three.

headlineQuote: I'm lucky, and I know it. My age, my savings and my curiosity all line up.
portrait: Erik (**58**, senior operator on a surface-mount electronics line) is curious and uses AI **every day** to find faults.
He is secure thanks to age, savings and a plan to stop around 62.
He separates thinking AI in 2028, which he welcomes, from **robots** in 2031, which shrink the number of seats.
He moves to mentoring and teaching the younger operators, and worries about colleagues like Ingrid and Sam.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries him most because the speed would hurt people who haven't touched the tools.
whatWouldHelp: Open **training** for everyone, run by firms and funded by the government.
